method:
Goal: a comparative, sequence-level picture of the ZRS limb enhancer across species whose orthologs Kvon et al. (2016) swapped into the mouse, to see what distinguishes the orthologs that supported normal limbs from the one that truncated them.

1. REFERENCE. The mouse ZRS was taken as the exact 1,324 bp interval Kvon et al. deleted by CRISPR, mm10 chr5:29,314,497-29,315,820 (their Figure S3), fetched from GRCm38.p6 NC_000071.6. Positive control that this is the right interval: the fetched sequence is exactly 1,324 bp and contains the paper's stated sgRNA recognition sequence (AGTACCATGCGTGTGTGTGA) on the minus strand at offset 16, i.e. 'in close proximity to its 5-prime border' as the paper describes; a 1-nt mutated copy of that motif is absent.

2. ORTHOLOG RETRIEVAL. Kvon et al. deposited NO GenBank accessions for the ZRS orthologs - the sequences are in supplementary Tables S2/S3 and the constructs were chemically synthesised - and those supplementary PDFs could not be retrieved (see limitations). Orthologs were therefore re-derived from public genomes: for each species the annotated LMBR1 locus (the ZRS lies in LMBR1 intron 5) was fetched with a 10 kb flank, and the ZRS was located inside it by unique 12-mer seeding from the mouse ZRS followed by local affine-gap alignment (Biopython PairwiseAligner). Where a snake had diverged so far from mouse that only a short block aligned, the Burmese python ZRS - itself mouse-anchored - was used as a bridging anchor; the anchor used is recorded per species. Human was taken from GRCh38 chromosome 7 and cross-checked against the dedicated RefSeq record NG_042169.2 ('Homo sapiens ZPA regulatory sequence (ZRS)'), which matches the fetched window exactly while a 1-nt mutant of it does not. King cobra came from scaffold183.1 of assembly AZIM01, the same king cobra assembly Kvon et al. used.

3. ALIGNMENT. All detected orthologs were aligned with MAFFT v7.525 L-INS-i, the same program and mode the paper used. The fetched 1.3 kb windows extend beyond the conserved enhancer, and in those flanks the sequences are not homologous at nucleotide resolution; MAFFT fills them with arbitrary gaps, which manufactures 'shared deletions' that are artefacts. (This was caught by eye: the non-snake blocks aligned there share no similarity with each other.) So, as Kvon et al. did with Gblocks, the alignment was trimmed to its alignable core and realigned: mouse positions were scored by column depth and conservation, smoothed over 31 positions, and the longest run with conservation >= 0.70 and depth >= 0.80 was kept. That core is mouse ZRS 398-1043 (646 bp), mm10 chr5:29,314,894-29,315,539. Every quantitative result below is computed on the realigned core.

4. MOTIFS. Each species' core was scanned on both strands with the JASPAR ETS1 matrix MA0098.3 (consensus ACCGGAAGTG), using a log-odds threshold derived by exact convolution of the score distribution under a uniform background so that p < 0.0032 means what it means in FIMO - the threshold Kvon et al. state. Controls: the consensus scores 15.94 bits and passes; poly-G, poly-C and poly-A all fail.

5. HUMAN DISEASE VARIANTS. All 694 ClinVar LMBR1 variants were fetched and filtered to those falling inside the human ZRS record's GRCh38 interval, then mapped through the alignment by coordinate arithmetic. No variant position was taken from memory or from prose.

retrievals.note: Interval is the 1,324 bp CRISPR deletion stated in Kvon et al. 2016 Figure S3; the fetched sequence contains the paper's sgRNA target on the minus strand at offset 16, which is the stated position near the 5' border.

RefSeq record NG_042169.2 ('Homo sapiens ZPA regulatory sequence (ZRS)') matches this chromosome window exactly at offset 2608, i.e. NC_000007.14:156,790,608-156,793,179; a 1-nt mutated copy of NG_042169.2 does not match, confirming the placement.

retrievals.source_kind: WGS scaffold183.1 of assembly AZIM01 (the king cobra assembly used by Kvon et al. 2016)

retrievals.note: NOT DETECTED. Scope of the negative: the whole annotated LMBR1 locus NC_142066.1:148621531-148710531 (89,001 bp, gene span +/-10 kb) was searched with unique 12-mer seeding plus local affine-gap alignment, using BOTH the mouse ZRS and the Burmese python ZRS as queries. Longest aligned block with the mouse query: 24 bp. Threshold for claiming a ZRS: 150 bp.

ets_scan.threshold_method: exact upper-tail of the score distribution by convolution
ets_scan.note: Kvon et al. used FIMO with ETS1 PWMs at p<0.0032; this is the same threshold and the same kind of model, but not the same software, and the site numbering E0-E4 of that paper is NOT reproduced here because their coordinates were not accessible. Every site is marked inferred.

e1_deletion.note: Independently recovered, not taken from the paper. Columns gapped in a species relative to lizard; the paper's 17 bp figure is also lizard-referenced ('a 17 bp sequence from the lizard ZRS ortholog was introduced into the python ZRS').

summary_table.knockin_phenotype_in_kvon2016: complete loss of Shh expression; truncation of both limb pairs

summary_table.note: no ZRS detected; excluded from the alignment

limitations: This is a correlational, post-hoc analysis of a handful of sequences. It is NOT a predictor. With two knock-in species that gave normal limbs and two that truncated, no statistic computed here has the power to establish that any sequence feature causes the phenotype; the causal evidence is Kvon et al.'s mouse knock-ins, not this alignment.

The sequences analysed are NOT the sequences Kvon et al. knocked in. Theirs were synthesised from supplementary Tables S2/S3, which could not be retrieved. These were re-derived from reference genomes, so they may differ from the constructs by assembly errors, strain or individual polymorphism, and by window boundaries.

Species substitutions were necessary and change what the comparison means: the paper used boa constrictor (Assemblathon 2 assembly, not in NCBI) and speckled rattlesnake Crotalus mitchellii (JPMF01); this analysis uses Eryx miliaris (dwarf sand boa, a different basal snake, from a dedicated GenBank ZRS record) and Crotalus tigris. Thamnophis elegans was added and is not in the paper at all. Viper (JTGP01) was not analysed.

Percent identity depends heavily on how much flanking sequence is included, and there is no single correct number. Mouse-human is 88.3% over the trimmed core, 78.6% over the full 1.3 kb window, and 85-86% over the best-aligning block alone. Kvon et al. state 73% for human vs mouse; they do not define the metric, so these numbers are NOT directly comparable to theirs and the discrepancy is a definitional difference, not a contradiction of either result.

The core boundaries (mouse 398-1043) come from thresholds on a smoothed conservation profile. The thresholds were chosen by reading the profile's shoulder, but they are choices, and the identity numbers shift if they move.

ETS site numbering E0-E4 from Kvon et al. is NOT reproduced. Their site coordinates were in inaccessible supplementary material, so no site here is claimed to be 'the' E1, E2 etc. Every motif call is marked inferred. The one exception in strength of evidence is the 17 bp deletion block, which was located independently by alignment and which the paper also describes as overlapping an ETS site.
A PWM hit is a sequence match, not a measurement of binding. No ChIP, EMSA or reporter data were used here, and FIMO itself was not run - an equivalent threshold was recomputed.

The corn snake negative ('no ZRS detected') is scoped: the whole annotated LMBR1 locus plus 10 kb either side was searched with 12-mer seeding and local alignment using BOTH the mouse and the Burmese python ZRS as queries. It does not exclude a ZRS remnant elsewhere in the corn snake genome, nor one too diverged for these queries to find.

Rattlesnake could not be assessed at the 17 bp site: MAFFT places unrelated sequence in those columns rather than a gap, so it is reported as not assessable there rather than as retaining the site. Its ETS1 scan returns no hit in that block.
Alignment of sequences this diverged is itself uncertain. Different aligners or parameters will move indel placement, and the snake columns are where that uncertainty is largest.
Model fidelity is not biological validity: reproducing Kvon et al.'s observations says these sequence relationships are real, not that any interpretation of limb loss built on them is.
